sections.heading: The Living World: Binomial Nomenclature & Taxonomic Hierarchy
sections.summary: Carolus Linnaeus proposed binomial nomenclature in Systema Naturae and Species Plantarum, assigning each organism a two-word Latinised scientific name governed by ICBN (botanical) and ICZN (zoological). Classification arranges taxa in an obligate ascending hierarchy where shared common characters decrease from Species to Kingdom.
keyPoints: Binomial rules: First word = Genus (Capital first letter), second word = specific epithet (lowercase); printed in italics or underlined separately when handwritten to denote Latin origin, with abbreviated author citation at the end (e.g., Mangifera indica Linn.).

Taxonomic hierarchy (ascending): Species -> Genus -> Family -> Order -> Class -> Phylum (animals) / Division (plants) -> Kingdom; Ernst Mayr defined biological species as reproductively isolated interbreeding populations.

Lower the category, greater the difficulty of determining relationships at higher levels? No: higher the category (Kingdom), greater is the difficulty of determining relationship to other taxa at the same level because fewer common characteristics exist.
NCERT Table 1.1 Exact Taxa — Man: Homo sapiens | Family Hominidae | Order Primata | Class Mammalia | Phylum Chordata; Housefly: Musca domestica | Muscidae | Diptera | Insecta | Arthropoda.
NCERT Table 1.1 Plant Taxa — Mango: Mangifera indica | Anacardiaceae | Sapindales | Dicotyledonae | Angiospermae; Wheat: Triticum aestivum | Poaceae | Poales | Monocotyledonae | Angiospermae.
Systematics (from Latin 'systema') includes identification, nomenclature, classification AND evolutionary (phylogenetic) relationships between organisms.

sections.heading: Whittaker's Five Kingdoms & Kingdom Monera
sections.summary: R.H. Whittaker (1969) established five kingdoms (Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia) using cell structure, body organisation, mode of nutrition, reproduction, and phylogenetic relationships. Kingdom Monera comprises exclusively prokaryotic microbes exhibiting the most extensive metabolic diversity.
keyPoints: Carl Woese's Three-Domain System splits Monera into Archaebacteria and Eubacteria (Bacteria) based on 16S rRNA and cell wall chemistry, placing all eukaryotes in Domain Eukarya.

Archaebacteria survive extreme habitats due to branched ether-linked membrane lipids and non-peptidoglycan (pseudomurein/protein) cell walls: Methanogens (obligate anaerobes in marshy areas & ruminant gut producing CH4), Halophiles (salty), Thermoacidophiles (hot sulphur springs).

Eubacteria possess rigid peptidoglycan (murein) cell walls; Cyanobacteria (BGA, e.g. Nostoc, Anabaena) have Chl a like green plants, gelatinous sheath, and specialised thick-walled HETEROCYSTS for anaerobic N2 fixation.

Chemosynthetic autotrophs (Nitrosomonas, Nitrobacter, Thiobacillus) oxidise inorganic NH3/NO2-/Fe2+/S to generate ATP for nutrient recycling (N, P, Fe, S); heterotrophic bacteria are the most abundant decomposers (curd Lactobacillus, antibiotics, N2-fixing Rhizobium).

Mycoplasma (PPLO) are the smallest living cells (~0.3 micrometre), completely LACK a cell wall (hence resistant to penicillin), are pleomorphic, and survive WITHOUT oxygen; pathogenic to plants and animals.

Bacterial reproduction is mainly binary fission; under unfavourable conditions they form endospores, and show primitive DNA transfer (conjugation/transformation/transduction) without true gametic fusion.

sections.heading: Kingdom Protista & Kingdom Fungi
sections.summary: Kingdom Protista groups all single-celled eukaryotes with membrane-bound organelles, bridging plants, animals, and fungi, while Kingdom Fungi consists of heterotrophic absorptive eukaryotes with chitin-polysaccharide cell walls. Fungal classification relies on mycelium septation, spore formation mode, and fruiting bodies.
keyPoints: Chrysophytes (Diatoms & Desmids/Golden algae): microscopic planktonic, chief producers in oceans; diatom cell walls form two overlapping silica-embedded shells like a soap box -> indestructible walls accumulate as gritty diatomaceous earth (polishing, oil/syrup filtration).

Dinoflagellates (mostly marine, photosynthetic): stiff cellulosic plates on outer surface, two flagella (one longitudinal, one transverse in furrow); Gonyaulax multiplies rapidly causing Red Tides releasing saxitoxin that kills marine fishes.

Euglenoids (freshwater stagnant, Euglena): lack cell wall, possess protein-rich flexible PELLICLE; two unequal flagella (one short, one long); mixotrophic (photosynthetic in sunlight with Chl a/b, predating heterotroph in dark).

Slime moulds (saprophytic protists): aggregate into multinucleate wall-less PLASMODIUM under favourable conditions, and differentiate into fruiting bodies bearing true cellulosic-walled spores dispersed by air currents during adversity.

Protozoans: Amoeboid (Entamoeba histolytica parasite, marine forms have silica shells), Flagellated (Trypanosoma -> sleeping sickness), Ciliated (Paramoecium -> coordinated cilia & gullet), Sporozoans (Plasmodium -> infectious sporozoite stage).

Fungi classes: Phycomycetes (aseptate coenocytic; Mucor, Rhizopus bread mould, Albugo parasitic on mustard; zoospores/aplanospores); Ascomycetes (septate branched; Saccharomyces unicellular, Aspergillus, Claviceps ergot, Neurospora genetic workhorse, edible morels & truffles; exogenous conidia, 8 endogenous ascospores in ascus); Basidiomycetes (septate dikaryotic, NO asexual spores, clamp connections; Agaricus mushroom, Ustilago smut, Puccinia rust; 4 exogenous basidiospores); Deuteromycetes (imperfect fungi, only asexual conidia known; Alternaria, Colletotrichum, Trichoderma).

sections.heading: Viruses, Viroids, Prions & Lichens (Non-Kingdom Entities)
sections.summary: Acellular infectious agents (viruses, viroids, prions) and dual symbiotic lichens find no place in Whittaker's five-kingdom system. NCERT tests exact scientist discoveries, nucleic acid types, and disease pairings.
keyPoints: Viruses are inert crystalline nucleoproteins outside host (obligate intracellular parasites): D.J. Ivanowsky (1892) recognised microbes smaller than bacteria causing tobacco mosaic; M.W. Beijerinck (1898) named extract 'Contagium vivum fluidum'; W.M. Stanley (1935) crystallised TMV.

No virus contains BOTH RNA and DNA: plant-infecting viruses (e.g., TMV) usually have single-stranded RNA (ssRNA); animal viruses have ssRNA, dsRNA, or dsDNA; Bacteriophages typically carry double-stranded DNA (dsDNA).

TMV capsid consists of 2,130 helically arranged protein subunits (capsomeres) protecting coiled ssRNA (~6400 nucleotides); T4 bacteriophage has tadpole head, collar, contractile sheath, and 6 tail fibres.
Viroids (discovered by T.O. Diener, 1971): free infectious low-molecular-weight ssRNA WITHOUT any protein coat (capsid), smaller than viruses, causing Potato Spindle Tuber Disease (PSTVd).

Prions: abnormally folded infectious proteins similar in size to viruses WITHOUT nucleic acid, causing Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE / Mad Cow disease) in cattle and Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease (CJD) in humans.

Lichens: mutually beneficial symbiosis between phycobiont (algal partner, autotrophic food provider) and mycobiont (fungal partner, shelter + water/mineral absorber); act as sensitive SO2 air pollution indicators (do not grow in polluted areas).

sections.heading: Plant Kingdom I: Algae & Bryophytes
sections.summary: Modern plant classification integrates cytotaxonomy, chemotaxonomy, and phylogenetic systems (Engler & Prantl, Hutchinson) beyond Linnaeus's artificial sexual system and Bentham-Hooker's natural system. Algae are mostly aquatic thalloid haplontic plants, whereas Bryophytes are amphibians of the plant kingdom with dominant haploid gametophytes.
keyPoints: Algal forms: colonial (Volvox), filamentous (Ulothrix, Spirogyra), massive marine kelps (Macrocystis up to 100 m); vegetative fragmentation, asexual zoospores, and sexual isogamy (flagellated Ulothrix, non-flagellated Spirogyra), anisogamy (Eudorina), and oogamy (Volvox, Fucus).

Chlorophyceae (Chlamydomonas, Volvox, Ulothrix, Spirogyra, Chara): Chl a, b; chloroplasts discoid/plate/reticulate/cup/spiral/ribbon with proteinaceous PYRENOIDS (protein core + starch sheath); inner cellulose + outer pectose cell wall; 2-8 equal apical flagella.

Phaeophyceae (Ectocarpus, Dictyota, Laminaria, Sargassum, Fucus): Chl a, c + fucoxanthin; food stored as laminarin & mannitol; cellulosic wall coated by gelatinous ALGIN; holdfast-stipe-frond body; pear-shaped gametes with 2 unequal laterally attached flagella.

Rhodophyceae (Polysiphonia, Porphyra, Gracilaria, Gelidium): Chl a, d + r-phycoerythrin (captures blue light in deep waters); Floridean starch (structurally similar to amylopectin & glycogen); cellulose-pectin-polysulphate ester wall yielding AGAR & CARRAGEEN; NO motile flagellated stages!

Bryophytes lack true roots/stem/leaves and vascular xylem/phloem; dependent on water for biflagellate antherozoids to reach flask-shaped archegonium; zygote (2n) forms multicellular SPOROPHYTE (foot, seta, capsule) nutritionally dependent on photosynthetic GAMETOPHYTE (n).

Liverworts (Marchantia: dorsiventral thallus, dioecious antheridiophore/archegoniophore, green multicellular asexual GEMMAE in gemma cups) vs Mosses (Funaria, Polytrichum, Sphagnum peat moss: creeping filamentous PROTONEMA -> upright leafy gametophore with multicellular branched rhizoids; elaborate capsule spore dispersal).

sections.heading: Plant Kingdom II: Pteridophytes & Gymnosperms
sections.summary: Pteridophytes are the first terrestrial vascular plants with an independent dominant diploid sporophyte (2n) and free-living inconspicuous haploid gametophyte (prothallus). Gymnosperms bear exposed ovules not enclosed in any ovary wall before or after fertilisation, lacking true fruits.
keyPoints: Pteridophyte classes: Psilopsida (Psilotum), Lycopsida (Selaginella, Lycopodium), Sphenopsida (Equisetum — horsetail with strobili), Pteropsida (Dryopteris, Pteris, Adiantum); leaves are microphylls (Selaginella) or macrophylls (ferns).

Homosporous pteridophytes (most ferns) produce monoecious prothalli requiring cool, damp, shady places for water-mediated fertilisation (restricting geographical spread), whereas Selaginella and Salvinia are HETEROSPOROUS (microspores & megaspores).
Seed habit precursor: In Selaginella and Salvinia, female gametophyte is retained on parent sporophyte for variable periods, where zygote develops into young embryo inside megasporangium.

Gymnosperms include medium/tall trees and shrubs (Sequoia sempervirens tallest redwood): taproots with fungal MYCORRHIZA in Pinus, or specialised N2-fixing CORALLOID ROOTS with cyanobacteria (Anabaena/Nostoc) in Cycas.

Cycas has unbranched stem, pinnate leaves (persisting years), and is dioecious (male cone & megasporophylls on separate plants; lacks female cone); Pinus has branched stem, needle leaves (thick cuticle, sunken stomata), and is monoecious (male & female cones on same tree).

Gymnosperm haploid endosperm (n) is the pre-fertilisation female gametophyte tissue carrying 2 or more archegonia; pollen grain reaches ovule via wind (anemophily) and forms pollen tube discharging male gametes near archegonia.

derivationsAndGraphs.title: Haplontic Life Cycle (Most Algae: Volvox, Spirogyra, Chlamydomonas)
derivationsAndGraphs.expressionOrCurve: Gametophyte (n) --[Mitosis]--> Gametes (n) --[Syngamy]--> Zygote (2n) --[Zygotic Meiosis]--> Spores (n) --> Gametophyte (n)
derivationsAndGraphs.keyTakeaway: Dominant photosynthetic phase is free-living haploid gametophyte; sporophytic generation is represented ONLY by the 1-celled diploid zygote (2n) with no free-living sporophyte.

derivationsAndGraphs.title: Haplo-Diplontic Life Cycle (Bryophytes, Pteridophytes, Ectocarpus, Polysiphonia, Kelps)
derivationsAndGraphs.expressionOrCurve: Gametophyte (n) --> Gametes (n) --> Zygote (2n) --[Mitosis]--> Multicellular Sporophyte (2n) --[Sporic Meiosis]--> Spores (n)
derivationsAndGraphs.keyTakeaway: Both phases are multicellular. Dominant phase is gametophyte (n) in Bryophytes (attached sporophyte) vs dominant independent sporophyte (2n) in Pteridophytes (independent prothallus n).

derivationsAndGraphs.title: Diplontic Life Cycle (Fucus, Gymnosperms, Angiosperms)
derivationsAndGraphs.expressionOrCurve: Sporophyte (2n) --[Gametic Meiosis]--> Haploid Gametes / Few-celled Gametophyte (n) --[Syngamy]--> Zygote (2n) --> Sporophyte (2n)
derivationsAndGraphs.keyTakeaway: Diploid sporophyte is dominant, photosynthetic, and independent; gametophytic phase is single-celled to few-celled (e.g., 3-celled pollen, 7-celled embryo sac).

derivationsAndGraphs.title: Fungal Dikaryophase Cycle (Ascomycetes & Basidiomycetes)
derivationsAndGraphs.expressionOrCurve: Haploid Hyphae (n) --[Plasmogamy]--> Dikaryon (n + n) --[Karyogamy]--> Diploid Zygote (2n) --[Meiosis]--> Haploid Spores (n)
derivationsAndGraphs.keyTakeaway: Unlike Phycomycetes where karyogamy follows plasmogamy immediately, Ascomycetes & Basidiomycetes exhibit a prolonged intervening dikaryotic (n + n) phase.

formulas.formula: Shared Characters: Species > Genus > Family > Order > Class > Phylum > Kingdom
formulas.note: Moving upward reduces common traits and increases difficulty of establishing inter-taxa links

formulas.formula: Chl a, b + Starch (Pyrenoids) + Cellulose/Pectose + 2-8 Equal Apical Flagella
formulas.note: Examples: Chlamydomonas, Volvox, Ulothrix, Spirogyra, Chara

formulas.formula: Chl a, c, Fucoxanthin + Mannitol/Laminarin + Algin + 2 Unequal Lateral Flagella
formulas.note: Examples: Ectocarpus, Dictyota, Laminaria, Sargassum, Fucus (Diplontic!)

formulas.formula: Chl a, d, r-Phycoerythrin + Floridean Starch + Polysulphate Esters + ZERO Flagella
formulas.note: Examples: Polysiphonia, Porphyra, Gracilaria, Gelidium (Agar sources)

formulas.formula: Ascospores = Endogenous (in ascus, 8) | Basidiospores = Exogenous (on basidium, 4)
formulas.note: Both have septate branched mycelium and a dikaryotic (n+n) phase

formulas.formula: Rhizoids, Protonema, Gemmae, Leafy axis = (n) | Foot, Seta, Capsule, SMC = (2n)
formulas.note: Spores formed inside capsule by meiosis are haploid (n)

formulas.formula: Root, Stem, Needle, Nucellus, Integument = (2n) | Endosperm, Pollen, Egg = (n)
formulas.note: Gymnosperm endosperm is PRE-fertilisation female gametophyte (n), NOT triploid!

formulas.formula: TMV (Plant) = ssRNA | Bacteriophage (T4) = dsDNA | Phi x 174 = ssDNA
formulas.note: Viroids = naked ssRNA (no capsid); Prions = infectious protein (no RNA/DNA)

formulas.formula: Heterosporous Pteridophytes = Selaginella & Salvinia (Micro + Megaspores)
formulas.note: Dryopteris, Pteris, Adiantum, Equisetum, Lycopodium are homosporous

formulas.formula: Algin (Brown algae) | Carrageen (Red algae) | Agar (Gelidium & Gracilaria)
formulas.note: Chlorella (unicellular green alga) is rich in protein & used as space food

comparison.title: Whittaker's Five Kingdoms NCERT Master Matrix

traps: Gymnosperm endosperm is HAPLOID (n) formed BEFORE fertilisation, whereas Angiosperm endosperm is TRIPLOID (3n) formed AFTER triple fusion — classic NEET Assertion-Reason trap!
Fucus is a Brown Alga (Phaeophyceae) yet exhibits a DIPLONTIC life cycle (NOT haplontic like Volvox or Spirogyra!), while Ectocarpus, Polysiphonia, and kelps are HAPLO-DIPLONTIC.
Archaebacteria cell walls do NOT contain peptidoglycan (murein); Mycoplasma has NO cell wall at all and still survives completely without oxygen.
Chlamydomonas and Chlorella were placed under Algae earlier, then shifted to Kingdom PROTISTA in Whittaker's 5-kingdom classification because they are unicellular eukaryotes!

In Bryophytes, the sporophyte is NOT independent or free-living (it is attached to and derives nourishment from the gametophyte), whereas in Pteridophytes BOTH gametophyte (prothallus) and sporophyte are independent.
Bryophytes have rhizoids (not true roots), while Gymnosperms have mycorrhiza in Pinus and coralloid roots with N2-fixing Anabaena/Nostoc in Cycas.

solvedExamples.question: Which combination of organism, cell wall material, and stored food reserve is completely accurate according to NCERT?
steps: Check Cyanobacteria (Nostoc): Prokaryotic Monera with peptidoglycan wall, Chl a, and cyanophycean starch (NOT floridean starch).
Check Diatoms (Chrysophytes): Silica-impregnated overlapping soap-box cell walls, chief ocean producers.
Check Laminaria (Phaeophyceae): Cellulose + algin wall; stores food as laminarin and mannitol.
Check Porphyra (Rhodophyceae): Floridean starch + Chl a, d + r-phycoerythrin + NO flagella.
solvedExamples.answer: Laminaria: Cellulose + algin wall, Laminarin/Mannitol reserve (and Porphyra: Floridean starch, no flagella)
solvedExamples.pitfall: Confusing algin (brown algae) with agar/carrageen (red algae) or Floridean starch (red algae) with mannitol (brown algae).

solvedExamples.question: Statement I: Viroids possess low molecular weight free RNA and lack a protein coat. Statement II: Prions contain abnormally folded proteins along with single-stranded RNA.
steps: Evaluate Statement I: T.O. Diener (1971) showed viroids causing Potato Spindle Tuber disease are free low-MW RNA without capsid -> Statement I is CORRECT.
Evaluate Statement II: Prions are pure infectious proteinaceous agents (causing BSE / CJD) that completely LACK nucleic acid (no RNA or DNA) -> Statement II is INCORRECT.
Match standard NEET option: Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
solvedExamples.answer: Statement I is correct, Statement II is incorrect
solvedExamples.pitfall: Assuming prions carry viral RNA alongside protein; prions have ZERO nucleic acid.

solvedExamples.question: A Marchantia gametophyte cell has 9 chromosomes (n = 9). Determine the chromosome number in (a) Gemma cell, (b) Foot cell of sporophyte, (c) Spore mother cell, and (d) Elater / Spore produced after meiosis.
steps: Gemmae are green, multicellular, asexual buds produced mitotically on the haploid gametophyte -> n = 9 chromosomes.
Foot, seta, capsule wall, and spore mother cells belong to the diploid sporophyte derived from the zygote -> 2n = 18 chromosomes.
Spores are produced by sporic meiosis of the diploid spore mother cell -> n = 9 chromosomes.
solvedExamples.answer: Gemma = 9, Foot = 18, Spore Mother Cell = 18, Spore = 9
solvedExamples.pitfall: Treating gemmae as diploid (2n) structures simply because they are multicellular buds.

solvedExamples.question: Match the plant structures to their organisms in NCERT diagrams: (A) Heterocyst in filament, (B) Gemma cup on thallus, (C) Strobilus + nodes/internodes, (D) Coralloid roots with N2-fixing cyanobacteria.
steps: (A) Nostoc (filamentous blue-green alga) shows specialised N2-fixing heterocyst surrounded by mucilaginous sheath.
(B) Marchantia (dioecious liverwort) bears cup-like gemma cups on dorsal thallus.
(C) Equisetum (Sphenopsida pteridophyte) shows rhizome, jointed stem with nodes/internodes, and terminal strobilus (cone).
(D) Cycas (unbranched gymnosperm) carries coralloid roots harbouring symbiotic cyanobacteria.
solvedExamples.answer: A-Nostoc, B-Marchantia, C-Equisetum, D-Cycas
solvedExamples.pitfall: Mixing up Selaginella (leafy microphyll stem with strobilus) with Equisetum (ringed nodes/internodes with whorled branches and terminal cone).

sections.heading: Root, Stem, Leaf Modifications & Inflorescence Types
sections.summary: Flowering plants display root systems (tap, fibrous, adventitious), stem architectures, and leaf phyllotaxy adapted to anchorage, storage, climbing, and photosynthesis. Inflorescence axis growth defines racemose versus cymose floral arrangement.
keyPoints: Root zones (tip upward): Root cap -> Region of meristematic activity (small thin-walled dense protoplasm) -> Region of elongation (responsible for root lengthening) -> Region of maturation (epidermal cells form unicellular ROOT HAIRS).

Root modifications: Tap storage (Carrot, Turnip), Adventitious storage (Sweet potato), Prop roots (Banyan), Stilt roots from lower nodes (Maize, Sugarcane), Pneumatophores growing negatively geotropically for O2 (Rhizophora in swampy areas).

Stem modifications: Underground food/perennation (Potato tuber, Ginger rhizome, Colocasia corm, Zaminkand), Tendrils from axillary buds (Cucumber, Pumpkin, Watermelon, Grapevine), Thorns from axillary buds (Citrus, Bougainvillea), Phylloclade photosynthetic stems (flattened Opuntia, cylindrical Euphorbia), Runner/Stolon/Offset (Pistia, Eichhornia)/Sucker (Banana, Pineapple, Chrysanthemum).

Leaf types & Phyllotaxy: Reticulate venation (Dicots) vs Parallel (Monocots); Pinnately compound (Neem) vs Palmately compound (Silk cotton) — petiole bears axillary bud (stipule/axil), leaflets NEVER have axillary buds!
Phyllotaxy: Alternate (1 leaf/node: China rose, Mustard, Sunflower), Opposite (2 leaves/node: Calotropis, Guava), Whorled (>2 leaves/node: Alstonia).

Inflorescence: Racemose (main axis continues growing, acropetal succession of flowers — Mustard, Pea) vs Cymose (main axis terminates in a flower, limited growth, basipetal succession — Solanum, Jasmine).

sections.heading: Floral Symmetry, Ovary Position, Aestivation & Placentation
sections.summary: A flower is a modified shoot where apical meristem transforms into floral meristem bearing four whorls (calyx, corolla, androecium, gynoecium). Exact NCERT terms and examples for symmetry, thalamus elevation, aestivation, and placentation are guaranteed MCQs.
keyPoints: Floral Symmetry: Actinomorphic (radial: Mustard, Datura, Chilli, China rose), Zygomorphic (bilateral: Pea, Gulmohar, Bean, Cassia), Asymmetric (irregular: Canna).

Ovary Position: Hypogynous / Superior ovary (Mustard, China rose, Brinjal); Perigynous / Half-inferior ovary (Plum, Rose, Peach — thalamus forms cup-like rim); Epigynous / Inferior ovary (Guava, Cucumber, Ray florets of Sunflower).

Aestivation (sepals/petals overlap): Valvate (margins just touch, no overlap: Calotropis), Twisted (regular one-margin overlap: China rose, Lady's finger, Cotton), Imbricate (irregular overlap, not in one direction: Cassia, Gulmohar), Vexillary/Papilionaceous (1 large posterior standard + 2 lateral wings + 2 anterior fused keel: Pea, Bean).

Stamen attachment & cohesion: Epipetalous (attached to petals: Brinjal, China rose), Epiphyllous (perianth: Lily); Monoadelphous (1 bundle: China rose), Diadelphous (2 bundles: Pea 9+1), Polyadelphous (>2 bundles: Citrus); Variation in filament length (Salvia, Mustard).
Carpel fusion: Apocarpous (free carpels: Lotus, Rose, Michelia) vs Syncarpous (fused carpels: Mustard, Tomato).

Placentation (ovule arrangement): Marginal (ridge along ventral suture: Pea), Axile (multilocular central axis: China rose, Tomato, Lemon), Parietal (inner wall, unilocular becoming bilocular via false septum REPLUM: Mustard, Argemone), Free Central (central axis, septa absent: Dianthus, Primrose), Basal (single ovule at base: Sunflower, Marigold).

sections.heading: Fruits & Seeds: Dicot, Monocot & Specialised Layers
sections.summary: Fertilised ovary ripens into fruit (pericarp + seeds), whereas parthenocarpic fruits (banana) develop without fertilisation. Comparing dicotyledonous and monocotyledonous seed coats, cotyledons, and endosperm persistence distinguishes key families.
keyPoints: Drupe fruit (develops from monocarpellary superior ovary, 1-seeded): Mango (thin epicarp, fleshy edible mesocarp, stony hard endocarp) and Coconut (fibrous mesocarp used for coir, stony endocarp, liquid free-nuclear + white cellular endosperm).

Dicot seed (Bean, Gram, Pea): Seed coat (outer testa, inner tegmen), hilum scar, micropyle pore, embryonal axis (plumule + radicle) and two fleshy cotyledons (generally non-endospermic EXCEPT Castor!).
Monocot seed (Maize, Wheat): Seed coat membranous and fused with fruit wall (Caryopsis); bulky starchy endosperm separated from embryo by proteinaceous ALEURONE LAYER (3n).
Monocot embryo features: Single large shield-shaped cotyledon called SCUTELLUM; short embryonal axis where plumule is enclosed in protective sheath COLEOPTILE and radicle in COLEORHIZA.
Perisperm (residual persistent diploid nucellus 2n): observed in Black pepper and Beet.

sections.heading: NMC Updated Plant Families I: Malvaceae & Cruciferae (Brassicaceae)
sections.summary: NMC UGMEB explicitly reinstated Malvaceae and Cruciferae alongside Leguminosae, Compositae, and Gramineae. Master their vegetative markers, floral formulas, stamen specialisations, placentation, fruits, and economic crops.
keyPoints: Malvaceae (Mallow family — China rose Hibiscus rosa-sinensis, Cotton Gossypium, Lady's finger/Okra Abelmoschus esculentus): Mucilage-rich stem, alternate stipulate leaves with stellate hairs, solitary axillary/cymose.

Malvaceae flower & formula: Bracteolate EPICALYX (3-7 bracteoles) below calyx; Actinomorphic, Bisexual; K_(5) valvate; C_5 twisted aestivation; Epipetalous MONOADELPHOUS stamens A_(infinity) forming staminal tube around style with kidney-shaped (reniform) MONOTHECOUS anthers.

Malvaceae gynoecium & fruit: Pentacarpellary to multicarpellary syncarpous SUPERIOR ovary G_(5-infinity) with AXILE placentation and capitate/branched stigmas; Loculicidal CAPSULE (Cotton/Bhindi) or Schizocarp fruit.

Cruciferae / Brassicaceae (Mustard family — Mustard Brassica campestris, Radish Raphanus, Turnip, Cabbage/Cauliflower Brassica oleracea): Pungent sulphur glucosinolate (myrosin) smell; Racemose (corymb) ebracteate flowers.

Cruciferae flower & formula: Actinomorphic, Bisexual; K_(2+2) (4 free sepals in 2 whorls); C_4 CRUCIFORM clawed petals arranged diagonally like a cross; A_(2+4) TETRADYNAMOUS stamens (2 short outer + 4 long inner).

Cruciferae gynoecium & fruit: Bicarpellary syncarpous SUPERIOR ovary G_(2); PARIETAL placentation starting unilocular and becoming bilocular via false septum REPLUM; SILIQUA (long, dehiscent from base upward) or SILICULA (short, Capsella) fruit.

sections.heading: NMC Updated Plant Families II: Leguminosae, Compositae & Gramineae
sections.summary: Leguminosae (Fabaceae), Compositae (Asteraceae), and Gramineae (Poaceae) represent the three largest angiosperm economic families in the NMC syllabus. Focus on papilionaceous vs capitulum vs spikelet morphology and unique fruits (legume, cypsela, caryopsis).
keyPoints: Leguminosae / Fabaceae (Pea Pisum sativum, Gram, Arhar, Moong, Soyabean, Groundnut, Indigofera, Sunhemp, Sesbania, Trifolium, Lupin, Muliathi): Root nodules with Rhizobium, pulvinus leaf base, pinnate/stipulate leaves, racemose.

Fabaceae flower & formula: Zygomorphic (%), Bisexual; K_(5) valvate/imbricate; C_(1+2+(2)) VEXILLARY corolla (1 standard vexillum + 2 wings alae + 2 fused keel carina); A_((9)+1) DIADELPHOUS stamens; Monocarpellary SUPERIOR ovary G_1 with MARGINAL placentation -> LEGUME pod, non-endospermic seed.

Compositae / Asteraceae (Sunflower Helianthus, Marigold Tagetes, Chrysanthemum, Parthenium): CAPITULUM (Head) inflorescence surrounded by involucre of bracts, bearing peripheral zygomorphic female/neuter RAY FLORETS and central actinomorphic bisexual DISC FLORETS.

Asteraceae flower & formula: Calyx modified into hairy/bristly PAPPUS (parachute wind dispersal); C_(5) tubular/ligulate; A_(5) epipetalous SYNGENESIOUS stamens (anthers fused into cylinder, filaments free); Bicarpellary syncarpous INFERIOR ovary G_(2) bar-above, single BASAL ovule -> CYPSELA fruit.

Gramineae / Poaceae (Wheat Triticum, Rice Oryza, Maize Zea, Sugarcane, Barley, Bamboo): Culm stem (hollow internodes, solid nodes), alternate leaf with sheathing base + LIGULE, parallel venation, SPIKE OF SPIKELETS inflorescence with sterile GLUMES + LEMMA (with awn) & PALEA.

Poaceae flower & formula: Zygomorphic (%), Bisexual (unisexual in Maize); Perianth reduced to 2 fleshy LODICULES (P_2); A_3 (6 in Rice/Bamboo) with VERSATILE dorsifixed anthers; Superior ovary G_1 with BASAL placentation & 2 FEATHERY stigmas -> CARYOPSIS fruit (pericarp fused with testa) + Scutellum.

sections.heading: Anatomy of Flowering Plants: Tissue Systems & Primary Organ Structure
sections.summary: Plant anatomy organizes cells into epidermal, ground, and vascular tissue systems, with primary dicot and monocot root/stem/leaf architectures exhibiting sharp diagnostic contrasts in stele, hypodermis, pith, and stomatal apparatus.
keyPoints: Epidermal tissue system: Cuticle (absent in roots!), Stomata (bean-shaped guard cells in dicots vs DUMBBELL-shaped guard cells in grasses/monocots!), unicellular root hairs vs usually multicellular shoot trichomes.

Vascular bundles: Radial (xylem & phloem on alternate radii = ROOTS) vs Conjoint (on same radius = STEMS & LEAVES); Open (cambium present = Dicot stem) vs Closed (cambium absent = Monocot stem/leaves); Exarch protoxylem = ROOTS vs Endarch = STEMS.

Dicot Root (Sunflower): Epiblema with root hairs, cortex, single-layered ENDODERMIS with suberin CASPARIAN STRIPS (waterproof band on tangential/radial walls), pericycle (lateral root origin), 2-4 xylem/phloem patches (diarch to tetrarch), small/inconspicuous pith, conjunctive tissue.
Monocot Root (Maize): Similar to dicot root EXCEPT polyarch (>6 xylem bundles), large well-developed pith, and NO secondary growth.

Dicot Stem (Sunflower) vs Monocot Stem (Maize): Dicot has collenchymatous hypodermis, starch sheath endodermis, semi-lunar sclerenchyma pericycle patches, RING of conjoint collateral OPEN vascular bundles, large pith; Monocot has sclerenchymatous hypodermis, NO pith/pericycle distinction, SCATTERED CLOSED vascular bundles with sclerenchymatous bundle sheath & protoxylem water-containing cavity!

Dorsiventral (Dicot) Leaf vs Isobilateral (Monocot) Leaf: Dicot has hypostomatic stomata (more on abaxial/lower epidermis) & differentiated mesophyll (upper palisade + lower spongy parenchyma); Monocot has amphistomatic stomata, undifferentiated mesophyll, and large empty colourless adaxial BULLIFORM CELLS in grasses that curl leaves inward during water stress to reduce transpiration.

traps: Syngenesious anthers (Compositae: anthers fused, filaments free) are the exact opposite of Monoadelphous/Diadelphous stamens (Malvaceae/Fabaceae: filaments fused, anthers free)!
Epigynous inferior ovary occurs in Guava, Cucumber, and Ray florets of Sunflower (Asteraceae), whereas Pea, Mustard, China rose, and Wheat all have Hypogynous SUPERIOR ovaries.
In Leguminosae, pea tendrils are LEAF/leaflet modifications, whereas in Cucumber/Pumpkin/Watermelon/Grapevine, tendrils are axillary STEM modifications!
Caryopsis (Poaceae) has pericarp completely fused with seed coat, whereas Cypsela (Asteraceae) is a dry indehiscent one-seeded fruit from an inferior bicarpellary ovary crowned by pappus.
Protoxylem is EXARCH in both Dicot and Monocot ROOTS, and ENDARCH in both Dicot and Monocot STEMS — never link exarch/endarch to dicot vs monocot!
Castor is a DICOT with ENDOSPERMIC (albuminous) seed, while Orchid is a MONOCOT with NON-ENDOSPERMIC seed — always beware absolute generalisations!

solvedExamples.question: Identify the angiosperm family characterised by spikelet inflorescence with glumes, perianth reduced to lodicules, versatile anthers, feathery stigmas, and caryopsis fruit.
steps: Lodicules represent reduced perianth scales unique to grasses.
Versatile anthers swinging freely on long filaments + plumose/feathery stigmas facilitate wind pollination (anemophily).
Caryopsis fruit (pericarp fused with testa) and scutellum identify Gramineae (Poaceae).
solvedExamples.answer: Gramineae (Poaceae)
solvedExamples.pitfall: Confusing pappus (hairy calyx in Compositae/Asteraceae) with lodicules (reduced perianth in Poaceae).

solvedExamples.question: Assertion (A): Mustard exhibits parietal placentation yet its ovary appears two-chambered at maturity. Reason (R): A false septum called replum develops across the unilocular ovary in Brassicaceae.
steps: Evaluate (A): Mustard (Brassica) bears ovules on the inner ovary wall (parietal) and becomes bilocular at maturity -> (A) is TRUE.
Evaluate (R): Cruciferae/Brassicaceae uniquely form a membranous false septum named replum dividing the single locule into two -> (R) is TRUE.
Confirm causal link: The replum directly causes the parietal unilocular ovary to appear two-chambered -> R correctly explains A.
solvedExamples.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
solvedExamples.pitfall: Confusing false septum (Replum in Mustard/Argemone) with true septa in Axile placentation (China rose/Tomato/Lemon).

solvedExamples.question: A typical maize seed shows 2n = 20 chromosomes in its root tip cells. Calculate the chromosome counts in its (a) Scutellum, (b) Aleurone layer, (c) Coleoptile, and (d) Perisperm (if present in a black pepper analogue with 2n = 20).
steps: Root tip = 2n = 20 -> n = 10.
Scutellum (embryonic cotyledon) and Coleoptile (plumule sheath) are diploid sporophytic tissues -> 2n = 20.
Aleurone layer is the outer protein-rich layer of endosperm -> triploid 3n = 30.
Perisperm is persistent nucellus -> diploid 2n = 20.
solvedExamples.answer: Scutellum = 20, Aleurone layer = 30, Coleoptile = 20, Perisperm = 20
solvedExamples.pitfall: Misclassifying the aleurone layer as part of the diploid pericarp (2n) instead of triploid endosperm (3n).

solvedExamples.question: In transverse section of a vascular bundle from a plant organ, xylem & phloem lie on the SAME radius, cambium is ABSENT, a sclerenchymatous bundle sheath surrounds it, and a water-containing lysigenous cavity appears below protoxylem. Identify the organ.
steps: Same radius = Conjoint bundle -> eliminates all Roots (radial bundles).
Cambium absent = Closed bundle -> eliminates Dicot Stem (open bundles with cambium).
Sclerenchymatous bundle sheath + protoxylem water-containing cavity in scattered bundles is the NCERT signature of a Monocot Stem (Maize).
solvedExamples.answer: Monocot Stem
solvedExamples.pitfall: Confusing Monocot Stem (conjoint closed with water cavity) with Monocot Root (radial polyarch with large pith).

sections.heading: Cell Theory & Prokaryotic Cell Architecture
sections.summary: Schleiden (1838) and Schwann (1839) formulated Cell Theory, completed by Rudolf Virchow (1855) with 'Omnis cellula-e cellula' (new cells arise from pre-existing cells). Prokaryotes lack membrane-bound organelles and nuclear envelope, packing circular genomic DNA and plasmids in a naked nucleoid.
keyPoints: Size benchmarks: Mycoplasma (0.3 micrometre), Bacteria (3-5 micrometre), Human RBC (7.0 micrometre diameter), Ostrich egg (largest isolated single cell), Nerve cell (longest).

Cell envelope (3 tightly bound layers): Glycocalyx (loose slime layer vs thick tough capsule) -> Cell wall (determines shape, prevents bursting) -> Plasma membrane (selectively permeable, structurally similar to eukaryotes).
Gram staining (Christian Gram): Gram-positive retain crystal violet stain vs Gram-negative lose it due to outer lipopolysaccharide differences.

Mesosomes: specialised infoldings of plasma membrane (vesicles, tubules, lamellae) helping cell wall formation, DNA replication & distribution, respiration, secretion, and surface area expansion; Chromatophores hold pigments in photosynthetic cyanobacteria.

Prokaryotic motility & attachment: Flagellum (filament longest, hook, basal body); Pili (elongated tubular pilin protein structures) & Fimbriae (small bristle-like fibres for attachment to rocks/host tissues) do NOT play a role in motility!

70S Ribosomes (50S + 30S; 15 nm x 20 nm) attach to single mRNA forming POLYRIBOSOME / POLYSOME; Inclusion bodies (phosphate granules, cyanophycean granules, glycogen granules, gas vacuoles in BGA/purple/green photosynthetic bacteria) are non-membrane bound.

sections.heading: Eukaryotic Cell Membrane, Cell Wall & Endomembrane System
sections.summary: Singer and Nicolson (1972) proposed the Fluid Mosaic Model where quasi-fluid phospholipid bilayers permit lateral movement of integral proteins. The Endomembrane System unites ER, Golgi apparatus, lysosomes, and vacuoles through coordinated vesicular trafficking.
keyPoints: Human erythrocyte (RBC) plasma membrane contains ~52% protein and ~40% lipids; Lipids are amphipathic phosphoglycerides (polar hydrophilic heads outside, hydrophobic tails inside); Cholesterol modulates fluidity.

Membrane proteins: Integral (buried partially/totally, cannot be easily extracted) vs Peripheral (lie on surface); Quasi-fluidity enables cell growth, intercellular junctions, secretion, endocytosis, and division.
Transport: Passive (simple diffusion, osmosis, facilitated via carrier proteins) vs Active (against concentration gradient using ATP, e.g., Na+/K+ pump).

Plant cell wall: Algae (cellulose, galactans, mannans, CaCO3); Higher plants (cellulose, hemicellulose, pectins, proteins). Middle lamella (calcium pectate glues neighbouring cells); Plasmodesmata traverse wall & middle lamella connecting cytoplasm.

Endomembrane System (ONLY ER + Golgi + Lysosomes + Vacuoles; Mitochondria, Chloroplasts & Peroxisomes are EXCLUDED!): Rough ER (80S ribosomes) -> protein synthesis/secretion; Smooth ER -> lipid & steroidal hormone synthesis.

Golgi Apparatus (Camillo Golgi 1898, flattened disc cisternae 0.5-1.0 micrometre): cis (convex/forming) receives ER vesicles -> trans (concave/maturing) modifies proteins/lipids into glycoproteins & glycolipids, and packs primary lysosomes (acid hydrolases active at acidic pH ~5); Plant tonoplast vacuole occupies up to 90% volume pumping ions AGAINST gradient.

sections.heading: Mitochondria, Plastids, Cytoskeleton, Cilia & Nucleus
sections.summary: Mitochondria and plastids are semi-autonomous endosymbiotic organelles carrying circular dsDNA, RNA, and 70S ribosomes. Eukaryotic motility and nuclear organisation rely on tubulin microtubules (9+2 / 9+0) and chromatin packaged into centromere-classified chromosomes.
keyPoints: Mitochondria (0.2-1.0 micrometre diameter, 1.0-4.1 micrometre length, Janus green stained): double membrane; inner membrane forms cristae housing ETS & F0-F1 oxysomes; matrix holds circular dsDNA, RNA, 70S ribosomes, and Krebs enzymes; divides by fission.

Plastids: Chloroplasts (Chl + carotenoids; stroma holds dsDNA, 70S ribosomes, Calvin enzymes; thylakoid stacks grana connected by stroma lamellae), Chromoplasts (fat-soluble carotenoids: carotene, xanthophylls), Leucoplasts (Amyloplasts = starch e.g. potato; Elaioplasts = oils/fats; Aleuroplasts = proteins).

Ribosomes (George Palade 1953, non-membrane bound RNA + protein): Eukaryotic 80S (60S + 40S) vs Prokaryotic/Organellar 70S (50S + 30S); 'S' = Svedberg unit measuring sedimentation coefficient (indirectly density & size).

Cilia & Flagella (9+2 axoneme): 9 peripheral microtubule DOUBLETS linked by radial spokes to central sheath enclosing 2 central singlets; emerge from basal body (centriole-like 9+0 triplets); Centrosome has 2 perpendicular centrioles surrounded by pericentriolar material.
Nucleus (Robert Brown 1831; chromatin named by Flemming using basic dyes): nuclear envelope with pores, nucleoplasm, non-membrane-bound NUCLEOLUS (site of active rRNA synthesis!).

Chromosomes by centromere position: Metacentric (middle, equal arms), Sub-metacentric (slightly away, 1 short p + 1 long q arm), Acrocentric (close to end, 1 extremely short + 1 very long arm), Telocentric (terminal centromere); Kinetochores are disc-shaped proteins on centromere; SAT-chromosomes have non-staining secondary constrictions.

sections.heading: Cell Cycle Phases: Interphase (G1, S, G2), G0 & Mitosis
sections.summary: Human cells divide roughly every 24 hours (yeast ~90 minutes), spending >95% of the cycle in metabolically active Interphase before entering short M-phase (~1 hour). Careful accounting separates DNA content (C) from chromosome count (N) at every stage.
keyPoints: G1 (Gap 1): Cell metabolically active, grows continuously, synthesises RNA/proteins, does NOT replicate DNA. G0 (Quiescent stage, e.g., adult heart cells): metabolically active, exits G1 without proliferating unless signalled.
S (Synthesis) Phase: DNA content DOUBLES (2C -> 4C), histone synthesis occurs, and centriole duplicates in animal cytoplasm, YET chromosome number (2n) remains UNCHANGED!
G2 (Gap 2): Tubulin and proteins synthesised in preparation for mitosis; mitochondria & plastids divide.

Mitosis (Equational Division) Karyokinesis: Prophase (chromosomal material condenses, centrosomes move to poles radiating asters, Golgi/ER/nucleolus/nuclear envelope disappear); Metaphase (complete nuclear envelope breakdown, chromosomes maximally condensed -> BEST stage to study morphology, aligned at metaphase plate via kinetochores).
Anaphase: Centromeres SPLIT simultaneously -> sister chromatids separate (now called daughter chromosomes) and migrate to opposite poles with centromeres leading and arms trailing.

Telophase & Cytokinesis: Chromosomes decondense at poles, nuclear envelope & nucleolus reform; Animal cytokinesis via centripetal cell furrow (microfilaments) vs Plant cytokinesis via centrifugal CELL PLATE (phragmoplast from Golgi -> middle lamella). Failure of cytokinesis after karyokinesis creates syncytium (liquid coconut endosperm).

sections.heading: Meiosis I & II: Prophase-I Substages & Gametogenic Reduction
sections.summary: Meiosis reduces diploid chromosome number (2n) to haploid (n) across two sequential nuclear divisions (Meiosis I reductional, Meiosis II equational) preceded by only a single S-phase. Prophase I drives homologous pairing and genetic recombination.
keyPoints: Leptotene: Chromosomes gradually become visible under light microscope as compaction continues throughout.
Zygotene: Homologous chromosomes pair longitudinally (SYNAPSIS) mediated by proteinaceous SYNAPTONEMAL COMPLEX, forming BIVALENT / TETRAD (1 bivalent = 2 homologous chromosomes = 4 chromatids).

Pachytene: Four chromatids of each bivalent become distinct tetrads; Recombination nodules appear -> CROSSING OVER (exchange of genetic segments) occurs between NON-SISTER chromatids of homologous chromosomes catalysed by enzyme RECOMBINASE!

Diplotene: Synaptonemal complex dissolves; recombined homologues separate EXCEPT at X-shaped crossover sites called CHIASMATA; in oocytes of some vertebrates, diplotene lasts months or years (dictyate arrest).

Diakinesis: Terminalisation of chiasmata, chromosomes fully condensed, meiotic spindle assembles, nucleolus & nuclear envelope break down -> transitions to Metaphase I (bivalents align on 2 equatorial plates).

Anaphase I vs Anaphase II: In Anaphase I, HOMOLOGOUS chromosomes separate while sister chromatids remain attached at undivided centromeres (2n -> n; 4C -> 2C); after short Interkinesis (NO DNA replication!), Meiosis II splits centromeres in Anaphase II (n -> n; 2C -> 1C), yielding 4 genetically distinct haploid cells.

comparison.title: Prophase-I Substages & Key Molecular Events
rows: Crossing over between NON-sister chromatids by Recombinase
X-shaped Chiasmata visible; oocyte arrest in vertebrates
Terminalisation of chiasmata; nuclear envelope disappears

traps: Mitochondria, Chloroplasts, and Peroxisomes are STRICTLY NOT part of the Endomembrane System because their functions are not coordinated with ER, Golgi, Lysosomes, and Vacuoles!
During S-phase, DNA quantity doubles (2C -> 4C) and centrioles duplicate in animal cytoplasm, YET chromosome number (2n) remains IDENTICAL to G1!
Pili and Fimbriae on bacteria are surface structures for conjugation/attachment and play NO role in motility (only flagella drive motility).
Crossing over in Pachytene happens between NON-SISTER chromatids of homologous chromosomes, NEVER between sister chromatids or non-homologous chromosomes.
In Anaphase-I, centromeres DO NOT split (homologous chromosomes separate keeping sister chromatids joined); centromeres split ONLY in Mitotic Anaphase and Meiotic Anaphase-II!
Centrioles duplicate during S-phase in cytoplasm (NOT inside nucleus) and lack any surrounding membrane, just like ribosomes and the nucleolus.

solvedExamples.question: A diploid meiocyte of Onion root/pollen mother cell has 2n = 16 chromosomes and 32 pg DNA at G1. Find (i) bivalents in Zygotene, (ii) chromatids in Metaphase-I, and (iii) chromosomes & DNA per daughter cell after Meiosis-I and Meiosis-II.

Post Meiosis-II: Centromeres split -> 8 chromosomes, 16 pg DNA per gamete.

sections.heading: Photosynthesis: Early Experiments, Pigments & Light Reactions
sections.summary: Photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical ATP and NADPH on chloroplast thylakoid membranes, driving CO2 reduction in the stroma. Historical experiments proved light, chlorophyll, CO2, and water's oxygen source (Cornelius van Niel).
keyPoints: Key experiments: Priestley (bell jar mint restores air), Ingenhousz (aquatic Hydrilla releases O2 bubbles ONLY in sunlight from green parts), Julius von Sachs (glucose stored as starch in green chlorophyll bodies), T.W. Engelmann (Cladophora + aerobic bacteria mapped first Action Spectrum peaking in Blue & Red!), van Niel (purple/green sulphur bacteria prove O2 comes from H2O using 18O isotope confirmation).

Pigments (chromatography): Chl a (bright/blue-green, chief reaction centre pigment), Chl b (yellow-green), Xanthophylls (yellow), Carotenoids (yellow to yellow-orange; accessory pigments broaden light absorption & prevent photo-oxidation of Chl a).

Photosystems: LHC (hundreds of antenna pigments) funnels energy to single Chl a reaction centre — PS-II has P680 (680 nm) located on appressed grana regions; PS-I has P700 (700 nm) on both grana and stroma lamellae!

Non-Cyclic Photophosphorylation (Z-scheme): PS-II absorbs 680 nm -> Pheophytin -> PQ -> Cytochrome b6f -> Plastocyanin (Cu) -> PS-I (P700) -> Ferredoxin -> NADP+ reductase (stroma side) -> produces ATP, NADPH, and O2.
Water splitting complex (associated with PS-II on the INNER LUMEN side of thylakoid membrane, needing Mn2+ and Cl-): 2H2O -> 4H+ + O2 + 4e-.

Cyclic Photophosphorylation (occurs in stroma lamellae which LACK PS-II and NADP+ reductase, or when only >680 nm light is available): cycles e- from PS-I -> Fd -> Cyt b6f -> PC -> PS-I -> synthesises ONLY ATP (NO NADPH, NO O2).

sections.heading: Chemiosmotic Hypothesis, Calvin (C3), Hatch-Slack (C4) & C2 Photorespiration
sections.summary: Peter Mitchell's Chemiosmotic Hypothesis explains thylakoid ATP synthesis via a steep lumen-to-stroma proton gradient. While C3 plants fix CO2 directly via RuBisCO (suffering photorespiration), C4 plants use spatial Kranz anatomy separation to concentrate CO2 around bundle-sheath RuBisCO.
keyPoints: Thylakoid proton gradient (lumen acidic, stroma alkaline) builds via 3 steps: (1) H2O splitting in lumen, (2) PQ pumping H+ from stroma to lumen across Cyt b6f, (3) NADP+ reductase consuming stromal H+ to make NADPH -> protons discharge through CF0-CF1 ATP synthase to stroma.

C3 Calvin Cycle (occurs in ALL photosynthetic plants — mesophyll in C3, bundle sheath in C4): (1) Carboxylation: RuBP (5C) + CO2 --(RuBisCO)--> 2 x 3-PGA (3C); (2) Reduction: uses 2 ATP + 2 NADPH per CO2; (3) Regeneration of RuBP: uses 1 ATP per CO2.
C3 stoichiometry: 1 CO2 = 3 ATP + 2 NADPH; 1 Glucose (6 turns) = 18 ATP + 12 NADPH; 1 Sucrose (12 turns) = 36 ATP + 24 NADPH.

Photorespiration (C2 cycle, C3 plants ONLY): When O2:CO2 is high or temperature rises, RuBisCO acts as oxygenase: RuBP + O2 -> 1 x 3-PGA (3C) + 1 x Phosphoglycolate (2C); shuttles across Chloroplast -> Peroxisome -> Mitochondria releasing CO2 and consuming ATP WITHOUT making sugar or ATP/NADPH (wastes ~25% fixed carbon!).

C4 Hatch-Slack Pathway (Maize, Sugarcane, Sorghum — Kranz anatomy with large thick-walled agranal bundle sheath cells): Mesophyll lacks RuBisCO, uses PEPcase to fix HCO3- + PEP (3C) -> OAA (4C) -> Malate (4C) -> transported to Bundle Sheath -> decarboxylated releasing CO2 for Calvin cycle + 3C Pyruvate returning to mesophyll (PPDK uses 2 ATP equivalents per CO2!).

C4 total cost: 5 ATP + 2 NADPH per CO2 (30 ATP + 12 NADPH per glucose); ZERO photorespiration, tolerate higher temperatures (30-40 deg C), higher light saturation; Blackman's Law of Limiting Factors: CO2 is usually limiting for C3 (saturates >450 uL/L; C4 saturates at ~360 uL/L!).

sections.heading: Cellular Respiration: Glycolysis, Fermentation & Link Reaction
sections.summary: Cellular respiration oxidises carbohydrates (or fats/proteins) via stepwise exergonic reactions conserving energy as ATP. Glycolysis (EMP pathway) occurs universally in the cytoplasm without oxygen, after which pyruvate enters fermentation or aerobic mitochondrial oxidation.
keyPoints: Glycolysis (Embden-Meyerhof-Parnas, 10 steps in Cytosol): Glucose (6C) -> 2 Pyruvate (3C); consumes 2 ATP (Hexokinase & Phosphofructokinase pacemaker) and produces 4 ATP (substrate-level phosphorylation at PGK & Pyruvate Kinase) + 2 NADH + H+ -> Net yield = 2 ATP + 2 NADH.
Sucrose entry into glycolysis: Invertase splits sucrose into Glucose + Fructose, both phosphorylated by Hexokinase entering the pathway.
Alcoholic Fermentation (Yeast, anaerobic): Pyruvate --(Pyruvate decarboxylase, TPP)--> Acetaldehyde + CO2 --(Alcohol dehydrogenase)--> Ethanol + NAD+; Yeast poisons itself when alcohol reaches ~13%.

Lactic Acid Fermentation (Bacteria Lactobacillus, exercising animal muscles under O2 deficit): Pyruvate --(Lactate dehydrogenase)--> Lactic acid (NO CO2 released!); both fermentations yield ONLY 2 net ATP (<7% of glucose energy!).
Link Reaction / Oxidative Decarboxylation (Mitochondrial Matrix): 2 Pyruvate + 2 NAD+ + 2 CoA --(Pyruvate Dehydrogenase, Mg2+, TPP, Lipoic acid, FAD)--> 2 Acetyl-CoA (2C) + 2 CO2 + 2 NADH + 2 H+.

sections.heading: Krebs Cycle, Mitochondrial ETS, ATP Balance Sheet & RQ
sections.summary: Acetyl-CoA enters the mitochondrial matrix Krebs (TCA) cycle generating reducing equivalents (NADH, FADH2) whose electrons descend Inner Mitochondrial Membrane ETS Complexes I-IV to drive Complex V ATP synthesis. Respiration is an amphibolic pathway serving both catabolism and anabolism.
keyPoints: Krebs Cycle (Matrix; ALL enzymes soluble EXCEPT Succinate Dehydrogenase bound to inner membrane!): Acetyl-CoA (2C) + OAA (4C) -> Citrate (6C) -> Isocitrate -> alpha-Ketoglutarate (5C, 1st CO2) -> Succinyl-CoA (4C, 2nd CO2) -> Succinate (GTP/ATP) -> Fumarate (FADH2) -> Malate -> OAA (3rd NADH). Per glucose (2 turns): 6 NADH + 2 FADH2 + 2 GTP(ATP) + 4 CO2.

ETS Complexes (Inner Mitochondrial Membrane): Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase, FMN + Fe-S), Complex II (Succinate dehydrogenase, FAD + Fe-S), Ubiquinone (UQ mobile hydrophobic carrier in membrane), Complex III (Cytochrome bc1), Cytochrome c (small mobile protein on OUTER surface of inner membrane!), Complex IV (Cytochrome c oxidase: Cyt a, a3 + 2 Cu centres CuA, CuB -> reduces 1/2 O2 + 2H+ -> H2O!).

Complex V (ATP Synthase): F0 integral channel + F1 peripheral catalytic headpiece; 4 H+ passing through F0-F1 from intermembrane space to matrix drive 1 ATP (NCERT classical textbook balance: 1 NADH = 3 ATP, 1 FADH2 = 2 ATP -> 38 ATP total in Malate-Aspartate shuttle / 36 ATP in Glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle).

Amphibolic Pathway: Respiratory intermediates are withdrawn for synthesis (Acetyl-CoA -> fatty acids/gibberellins; alpha-Ketoglutarate -> glutamate; Succinyl-CoA -> chlorophyll/haem; OAA -> aspartate).

Respiratory Quotient (RQ = Vol CO2 evolved / Vol O2 consumed): Carbohydrates = 1.0; Fats (Tripalmitin: 102 CO2 / 145 O2) = 0.7; Proteins = ~0.9; Organic acids (Oxalic = 4.0, Malic = 1.33) > 1; Succulents/CAM at night = 0; Anaerobic = infinity.

sections.heading: Plant Growth Kinetics, Differentiation & Plasticity
sections.summary: Plant growth is indeterminate due to open meristems and measurable via fresh/dry weight, length, area, volume, or cell number. Living plant cells exhibit remarkable developmental reversibility (dedifferentiation and redifferentiation) and environmentally induced morphological plasticity.
keyPoints: Phases of growth: Meristematic (dense protoplasm, conspicuous nuclei, thin primary cellulosic walls with abundant plasmodesmata), Elongation (vacuolation, cell enlargement, new wall deposition), Maturation (maximal wall thickening & protoplasmic modifications).
Arithmetic growth (constant rate, e.g., root elongating at constant rate; one daughter cell divides, other differentiates): L_t = L_0 + r*t (linear graph).

Geometric / Exponential growth (both progeny divide, typical microbial/embryo early phase): W_1 = W_0 * e^(rt), yielding J-curve initially and S-shaped Sigmoid curve (Lag -> Log/Exponential -> Stationary) under nutrient limits.
Growth Rates: Absolute Growth Rate (AGR = total growth per unit time) vs Relative Growth Rate (RGR = growth per unit time / initial parameter).

Differentiation (meristematic -> specialised permanent cell, e.g., tracheary element loses protoplasm & develops lignocellulosic secondary wall) -> Dedifferentiation (mature living parenchyma regains division capacity -> interfascicular cambium, cork cambium) -> Redifferentiation (cambial derivatives mature into secondary xylem/phloem/cork).

Plasticity (different pathways in response to environment or life phase): Heterophylly in Cotton, Coriander, Larkspur (developmental), and Buttercup / Ranunculus (environmental aquatic vs terrestrial leaves).

sections.heading: Plant Growth Regulators (Auxin, GA, Cytokinin, Ethylene & ABA)
sections.summary: Five classic phytohormones regulate plant growth and stress responses: promoters (Auxin, Gibberellins, Cytokinins) and inhibitors/ripening regulators (Abscisic Acid, gaseous Ethylene). NCERT bioassays, chemical natures, and agricultural applications are routinely tested.
keyPoints: Auxins (Indole-3-acetic acid IAA, IBA natural; NAA, 2,4-D synthetic; Charles & Francis Darwin canary grass coleoptile phototropism; F.W. Went isolated auxin from Avena oat coleoptile tips!): Apical dominance (removed by decapitation in tea/hedges), rooting in stem cuttings, parthenocarpy in Tomatoes, prevents premature fruit/leaf drop (promotes drop of OLDER mature leaves/fruits), 2,4-D kills dicot weeds selectively leaving monocot lawns, xylem differentiation.

Gibberellins (>100 known, GA1, GA2, GA3 most studied acidic terpenes; Kurosawa 1926 'Bakanae' foolish seedling disease in rice caused by Gibberella fujikuroi): Internode elongation (BOLTING in rosette plants like Beet, Cabbage; increases Sugarcane stem length +20 tonnes/acre!), increases apple size/shape, delays senescence (fruits stay longer on tree), speeds malting in brewing, promotes early seed production in juvenile conifers.

Cytokinins (Adenine derivatives; Skoog & Miller isolated KINETIN from autoclaved herring sperm DNA — synthetic; Zeatin from corn kernels & coconut milk — natural): Promotes cytokinesis, overcomes apical dominance (promotes lateral shoot growth!), produces new leaves/chloroplasts, adventitious shoot formation, delays leaf senescence via nutrient mobilisation (Richmond-Lang effect).

Ethylene (Gaseous C2H4; Cousins confirmed ripened oranges hastened banana ripening): Horizontal growth of seedlings, swelling of axis, apical hook formation in dicot seedlings (Triple Response); senescence & abscission; RESPIRATORY CLIMACTERIC burst in fruit ripening; breaks seed/bud dormancy (peanut sprouting, potato tuber sprouting); rapid internode/petiole elongation in deep-water rice; promotes femaleness in CUCUMBER; thinning in cotton, cherry, walnut (Ethephon source).

Abscisic Acid (ABA — Carotenoid derivative, 'Stress Hormone'): General growth & metabolism inhibitor; stimulates rapid STOMATAL CLOSURE during water stress; inhibits seed germination & induces SEED DORMANCY (antagonises GA!); promotes abscission.

traps: Bundle sheath cells of C4 plants possess AGRANAL chloroplasts (lack grana/PS-II, rich in RuBisCO) so they DO NOT evolve O2, preventing RuBisCO oxygenase waste!

solvedExamples.question: Which mitochondrial respiratory complex contains two copper centres (Cu_A and Cu_B) along with cytochromes a and a3, and directly transfers electrons to oxygen?
steps: Recall NCERT Ch 14 Respiration ETS complexes I to IV.
Complex I = NADH dehydrogenase; Complex II = Succinate dehydrogenase; Complex III = Cytochrome bc1.
Complex IV = Cytochrome c oxidase containing cytochromes a, a3 and TWO copper centres, reducing O2 to H2O.

solvedExamples.question: Compare total ATP and NADPH consumed to fix 12 molecules of CO2 into 1 molecule of Sucrose in (a) Wheat (C3) and (b) Sugarcane (C4).
steps: 12 CO2 molecules = 12 turns of Calvin cycle (2 glucose equivalents = 1 sucrose).
Wheat (C3): 3 ATP + 2 NADPH per CO2 -> 12 x (3 ATP + 2 NADPH) = 36 ATP + 24 NADPH.
Sugarcane (C4): 5 ATP + 2 NADPH per CO2 (3 in bundle sheath + 2 in mesophyll PPDK) -> 12 x (5 ATP + 2 NADPH) = 60 ATP + 24 NADPH.
solvedExamples.answer: Wheat (C3): 36 ATP + 24 NADPH | Sugarcane (C4): 60 ATP + 24 NADPH
solvedExamples.pitfall: Forgetting that NADPH demand (2 per CO2 = 24 per sucrose) stays identical in C3 and C4; only ATP rises from 36 to 60!

solvedExamples.question: Two leaves A (initial area 5 cm^2) and B (initial area 50 cm^2) both grow by +5 cm^2 in one day. Calculate their Absolute Growth Rates (AGR) and Relative Growth Rates (RGR).
steps: AGR = Change in area / time -> Leaf A = 5 cm^2/day; Leaf B = 5 cm^2/day (identical AGR).
RGR = (Change in area / Initial area) x 100 -> Leaf A = (5 / 5) x 100 = 100% per day.
Leaf B RGR = (5 / 50) x 100 = 10% per day.
solvedExamples.answer: Both have AGR = 5 cm^2/day; RGR of A = 100%/day vs RGR of B = 10%/day

sections.heading: Male Reproductive Organ: Stamen, Microsporangium & Pollen Grain
sections.summary: A typical angiosperm stamen comprises a slender filament and a bilobed, dithecous, tetrasporangiate anther. Four microsporangial wall layers protect and nourish developing haploid microspores via meiosis in diploid sporogenous tissue.
keyPoints: Anther wall layers (outside to inside): Epidermis -> Endothecium (fibrous callose thickenings for dehiscence) -> Middle layers (1-3 ephemeral layers) -> Tapetum (innermost, dense cytoplasm, often >1 nucleus / polyploid, nourishes pollen & secretes sporopollenin precursors/Ubisch bodies + pollenkitt).
Microsporogenesis: Each diploid cell of sporogenous tissue acts as Pollen Mother Cell (PMC, 2n) undergoing meiosis to produce a haploid microspore tetrad (n) held by callose, dissociated by callase.

Pollen grain (25-50 micrometre): Outer EXINE made of SPOROPOLLENIN (most resistant organic material known — resists high temp, strong acids/alkalis, zero enzymes degrade it; absent at GERM PORES for pollen tube emergence) + inner INTINE (thin, continuous, cellulose + pectin).

2-celled vs 3-celled shedding: Asymmetric mitosis produces a large VEGETATIVE cell (abundant food reserve, large irregular nucleus) and small spindle-shaped GENERATIVE cell (floats in vegetative cytoplasm). Over 60% angiosperms shed at 2-celled stage; remaining 40% divide generative cell mitotically into 2 male gametes BEFORE shedding (3-celled stage).

Pollen allergy & viability: Carrot grass (Parthenium, imported as contaminant with wheat) causes severe pollen allergy/asthma; Pollen viability = ~30 minutes in cereals (Rice, Wheat) vs months in Rosaceae, Leguminosae, Solanaceae; Stored in liquid nitrogen (-196 deg C) in pollen banks.

sections.heading: Female Reproductive Organ: Pistil, Ovule & 7-Celled 8-Nucleate Embryo Sac
sections.summary: The gynoecium ranges from monocarpellary to multicarpellary (apocarpous in Michelia vs syncarpous in Papaver). Each anatropous ovule differentiates a single diploid Megaspore Mother Cell that forms a monosporic Polygonum-type embryo sac.
keyPoints: Anatropous ovule parts: Funicle (stalk), Hilum (junction of ovule & funicle), Protective Integuments (1 or 2) leaving opening MICROPYLE (chalazal end opposite micropylar pole), diploid NUCELLUS (abundant reserve food).
Megasporogenesis: Single diploid Megaspore Mother Cell (MMC, 2n) differentiates in micropylar nucellus -> meiosis -> linear tetrad of 4 haploid megaspores (n).

Monosporic development (Polygonum type): 3 micropylar megaspores degenerate; ONLY 1 functional CHALAZAL megaspore undergoes 3 sequential STRICTLY FREE-NUCLEAR mitotic divisions (2 -> 4 -> 8 nuclei) before cell wall formation!

Mature Embryo Sac (7-Celled, 8-Nucleate): Micropylar end = Egg Apparatus (1 Egg cell n + 2 Synergids n with cellular thickenings called FILIFORM APPARATUS guiding pollen tube!); Chalazal end = 3 Antipodals (n); Central Cell = 1 large cell with 2 Polar Nuclei (n + n) fusing later to form secondary nucleus (2n).
Ovule count per ovary examples: Single ovule (Wheat, Paddy, Mango) vs Many ovules (Papaya, Watermelon, Orchids).

sections.heading: Pollination Mechanisms, Agents & Outbreeding Devices
sections.summary: Because both male and female angiosperm gametes are non-motile, pollination transfers pollen to stigma via abiotic (wind/water) or biotic (insect/bird/bat) agents. Plants deploy structural, temporal, and genetic outbreeding barriers to prevent inbreeding depression.
keyPoints: Three pollination types: Autogamy (same flower: Viola, Oxalis, Commelina produce BOTH open Chasmogamous & closed Cleistogamous flowers guaranteeing seed set!), Geitonogamy (different flower, SAME plant — functionally cross-pollination with agent, genetically autogamy!), Xenogamy (different plants -> true genetic variation).

Abiotic agents (~20% families; wind more common than water): Anemophily (grasses, corn cob tassels = stigma & style; light non-sticky pollen, well-exposed stamens, feathery stigma, single ovule per ovary, numerous flowers in inflorescence); Hydrophily (~30 genera, mostly monocots): Vallisneria (freshwater epihydrophily — female flower reaches surface on long stalk) & Zostera seagrass (marine hypohydrophily — long ribbon-like pollen with mucilaginous covering); Water hyacinth & Water lily are insect/wind pollinated!

Biotic agents (80% pollination by insects, bees dominant): Colourful, fragrant, nectar-rich, sticky pollen; Floral rewards (nectar, pollen, safe egg-laying sites in 6-ft Amorphophallus & Yucca-Pronuba moth obligate mutualism!).

Outbreeding devices (discourage self-pollination): (1) Non-synchronised pollen release & stigma receptivity (Dichogamy), (2) Spatial separation of anther & stigma (Herkogamy), (3) Genetic SELF-INCOMPATIBILITY (pollen fails to germinate/grow on same flower/plant pistil), (4) Unisexuality: Monoecious (Castor, Maize — prevents autogamy, NOT geitonogamy!) vs Dioecious (Papaya — prevents BOTH autogamy AND geitonogamy!).
Pollen robbers / nectar thieves: Many insects consume pollen or nectar WITHOUT bringing about pollination (no co-evolved reward transfer).

sections.heading: Pollen-Pistil Interaction, Artificial Hybridisation & Double Fertilisation
sections.summary: The pistil executes chemical dialogue to accept compatible pollen and reject incompatible or wrong-species pollen. Upon siphonogamous pollen tube entry into a synergid, angiosperms uniquely execute Double Fertilisation (Syngamy + Triple Fusion).
keyPoints: Pollen-pistil recognition: Chemical components mediate pistil acceptance; compatible pollen germinates through germ pore forming pollen tube carrying 2 male gametes (generative cell divides during tube growth if shed at 2-celled stage).
Pollen tube enters ovule through micropyle (porogamy), guided by FILIFORM APPARATUS into ONE of the two synergids (which degenerates), releasing 2 male gametes into synergid cytoplasm.

Artificial hybridisation: Emasculation (removal of anthers from bisexual female-parent flower BEFORE anther dehiscence using forceps; UNNECESSARY in unisexual female flowers!) + Bagging (butter paper bag prevents unwanted pollen contamination) + Rebagging after dusting desired pollen.

Double Fertilisation (discovered by Nawaschin; UNIQUE to Angiosperms!): (1) SYNGAMY: 1st male gamete (n) + Egg cell (n) -> Zygote (2n) -> Embryo; (2) TRIPLE FUSION: 2nd male gamete (n) + 2 Polar Nuclei (n + n) -> Primary Endosperm Nucleus (PEN, 3n) inside Primary Endosperm Cell (PEC) -> Endosperm.
In vitro pollen germination: Easily demonstrated by dusting pollen (pea, chickpea, Crotalaria, balsam, Vinca) on a glass slide in ~10% sugar solution for 15-30 minutes.

sections.heading: Post-Fertilisation: Endosperm, Dicot & Monocot Embryogeny
sections.summary: Endosperm development precedes embryogeny to guarantee nutrition for the dividing zygote. Dicot and monocot embryos diverge early after the globular and heart-shaped proembryo stages in cotyledon number and protective sheaths.
keyPoints: Endosperm types: Free-nuclear (most common initially: successive nuclear divisions without walls, e.g., tender Coconut water = thousands of free nuclei) followed by cellularisation (surrounding white coconut kernel = cellular endosperm!).

Albuminous / Endospermic seeds (retain endosperm): Wheat, Maize, Barley, Castor (dicot!), Coconut; Non-albuminous / Exalbuminous seeds (endosperm completely consumed by embryo): Pea, Groundnut, Beans, Orchid (monocot!).

Embryogeny (at micropylar end): Zygote (2n) -> Proembryo -> Globular -> Heart-shaped -> Mature embryo; Dicot embryo has embryonal axis + 2 cotyledons (epicotyl above cotyledon node ending in plumule; hypocotyl below ending in radicle + root cap).

Monocot grass embryo: Single shield-shaped lateral cotyledon = SCUTELLUM; lower radicle + root cap enclosed in undifferentiated sheath COLEORHIZA; hollow foliar sheath enclosing shoot apex & leaf primordia = COLEOPTILE; epiblast = reduced 2nd cotyledon remnant.
Early embryogeny similarity: Initial stages of embryo development (proembryo -> globular -> heart-shaped) are similar in both monocots and dicots before cotyledon divergence.

sections.heading: Seed, Fruit Classification, Viability, Apomixis & Polyembryony
sections.summary: The ovule matures into a seed (10-15% moisture dormancy) and the ovary into a fruit, providing dispersal, protection, and genetic variation. Special asexual seed mechanisms like apomixis fix hybrid vigour without segregation.
keyPoints: Ovule -> Seed; Integuments -> Seed coats (Testa & Tegmen); Micropyle -> water & O2 entry pore during germination; Ovary -> Fruit; Ovary wall -> Pericarp; Persistent nucellus -> Perisperm (Black pepper, Beet).

True fruits (develop strictly from ovary: Mango, Tomato) vs False fruits (thalamus also contributes to fleshy fruit: Apple, Strawberry, Cashew) vs Parthenocarpic fruits (seedless fruits formed WITHOUT fertilisation, e.g., Banana, or induced by Auxin/GA).

Seed longevity records (NCERT exact): Lupinus arcticus (arctic tundra) germinated after 10,000 years dormancy; Phoenix dactylifera (date palm excavated at King Herod's palace near Dead Sea) viable after 2,000 years!
High-seed-count fruits: Orchids (thousands of tiny seeds per fruit) and parasitic species Orobanche & Striga, plus Ficus.

Apomixis (Asteraceae & grasses): Production of seeds WITHOUT fertilisation (mimics sexual reproduction): diploid egg cell forms without reduction division OR diploid nucellar cells protrude into embryo sac -> fixes hybrid traits permanently in hybrid seed industry so farmers don't buy costly hybrid seeds yearly!
Polyembryony: Presence of more than one embryo in a single seed — classic NCERT examples: Citrus and Mango (sporophytic budding from diploid nucellar/integumentary cells).

rows: NOT prevented by Monoecious (Castor/Maize); Prevented ONLY by Dioecious (Papaya)

traps: Monoecious plants like Castor and Maize prevent Autogamy ONLY — they STILL undergo Geitonogamy! ONLY Dioecious plants (like Papaya) prevent BOTH Autogamy and Geitonogamy!
Water hyacinth and Water lily are AQUATIC plants yet are pollinated by INSECTS or WIND (flowers emerge above water), NOT by water!

solvedExamples.question: Which statement correctly describes the ploidy and developmental origin of coconut water and the surrounding white kernel?
steps: Coconut endosperm originates from the triploid Primary Endosperm Nucleus (PEN, 3n) formed by triple fusion.
Tender coconut water is free-nuclear liquid endosperm (thousands of triploid nuclei).
The edible white kernel is cellular endosperm formed later by cytokinesis around free nuclei.
solvedExamples.answer: Both coconut water (free-nuclear) and white kernel (cellular) are triploid (3n) endosperm
solvedExamples.pitfall: Confusing free-nuclear coconut water with haploid female gametophyte or nucellar perisperm.

solvedExamples.question: Statement I: Dioecious plants like Papaya prevent both autogamy and geitonogamy. Statement II: Monoecious plants like Maize prevent both autogamy and geitonogamy.
steps: Papaya has male and female flowers on separate plants -> neither autogamy nor geitonogamy is possible -> Statement I is CORRECT.
Maize has separate male (tassel) and female (cob) flowers on the SAME plant -> prevents autogamy, but pollen from tassel can pollinate cob on the same plant (geitonogamy).
Therefore Statement II is INCORRECT because monoecious plants only stop autogamy.
solvedExamples.answer: Statement I is correct, Statement II is incorrect
solvedExamples.pitfall: Thinking unisexual flowers on the same monoecious plant eliminate geitonogamy.

solvedExamples.question: If a tetraploid (4n) female plant is pollinated by a hexaploid (6n) male plant, find the ploidy of (a) Embryo, (b) Endosperm, (c) Seed coat, and (d) Perisperm.
steps: Female gamete (egg & each polar nucleus) = 4n / 2 = 2n; Male gamete = 6n / 2 = 3n.
Embryo (Zygote) = Egg (2n) + Male (3n) = 5n.
Endosperm (PEN) = Two Polar Nuclei (2n + 2n) + Male (3n) = 7n.
Seed coat (integuments) and Perisperm (nucellus) are strictly maternal sporophytic tissues -> 4n.
solvedExamples.answer: Embryo = 5n, Endosperm = 7n, Seed coat = 4n, Perisperm = 4n
solvedExamples.pitfall: Assuming seed coat/perisperm changes ploidy after cross-pollination (maternal tissues stay 4n).

solvedExamples.question: Identify the labelled parts of a Grass (Monocot) Embryo from top to bottom in the NCERT L.S. diagram: (A) Shield-shaped cotyledon, (B) Hollow foliar sheath around shoot apex, (C) Undifferentiated sheath enclosing radicle, (D) Small remnant opposite scutellum.
steps: (A) Lateral shield-shaped single cotyledon = Scutellum.
(B) Foliar sheath enclosing shoot apex & few leaf primordia = Coleoptile.
(C) Undifferentiated sheath enclosing radicle & root cap = Coleorhiza.
(D) Reduced second cotyledon flap opposite scutellum = Epiblast.
solvedExamples.answer: A-Scutellum, B-Coleoptile, C-Coleorhiza, D-Epiblast
solvedExamples.pitfall: Swapping Coleoptile (shoot/plumule cover) and Coleorhiza (root/radicle cover).
